entry.title: Vivian Chang talks about design in engineering

media:group.media:title: Vivian Chang talks about design in engineering
media:group.media:description:
Vivian Chang ‘28 knows that learning to design is learning to pay attention. Design in engineering is more than just making something look good; as she discusses in this video, it’s about solving real-world problems. She took “EGR 107: Design Fundamentals,” offered by the Keller Center, which teaches you to frame problems, come up with ideas, and test them with prototypes. Along the way, you start seeing the world differently and questioning the systems we inherit. It's also where Princeton's new minor in design starts.
The minor pulls from all over campus, including engineering, computer science, architecture, theater, music, anthropology, and sociology, and you finish with a portfolio you can show. There’s no design experience needed, and it’s open to every major. Add EGR 107: Design Fundamentals to your spring schedule. Follow this URL for more information: https://kellercenter.princeton.edu/academics/design?utm_medium=social&utm_source=linktree&utm_campaign=kellercenter.princeton.edu

entry.title: Princeton-Intel Research Experience for Undergraduates Program

media:group.media:title: Princeton-Intel Research Experience for Undergraduates Program
media:group.media:description:
What happens when the next generation of researchers takes on real-world cybersecurity challenges? 🔐
The sixth annual Princeton-Intel Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) Program brought six rising juniors from across the country to Princeton for a summer of hands-on research alongside faculty and graduate student mentors from Princeton Engineering and industry mentors from Intel.
This summer, students explored how advanced analysis techniques, including artificial intelligence and formal methods, can make complex computing systems more secure, efficient and easier to design.
🎥 Hear from ECE professor Sharad Malik about why the program was created and from Princeton undergraduate Jessica Hou about her summer research alongside ECE professor Prateek Mittal. Plus, hear from the mentors helping prepare the next generation of cybersecurity researchers and leaders.
A special thank-you to Princeton faculty members Maria Apostolaki and Aarti Gupta; Intel program manager Bo-Yuan Huang and Jason Fung; and all the Intel industry mentors, graduate students and staff who made this summer’s program possible.
Interested in joining the 2027 cohort? Learn more: https://lnkd.in/gk4EpcTw

media:group.media:title: Helping robots learn like toddlers
media:group.media:description:
This robot can be trained to wave hello, or do any other simple motion, by moving it around manually and programming it to repeat the motion on command. But a group of students in the Princeton Vision and Learning Lab are working on training the robot to learn like any toddler would: by trial and error. It’s called “reinforcement learning,” in which the robot is incentivized to take actions that will get it to do useful tasks.
The team is led by Professor Jia Deng of the Department of Computer Science, and includes eight undergraduates and grad student Erich Liang, who you see in this video filmed in the Robotics Lab.
The robot uses artificial intelligence so it can explore a simulated environment, and learn on its own like a human would in the real world, building on its mistakes.
“The more realistic the simulated environment is, the more likely it is to succeed in the real world,” Liang said.
To learn more about the Vision and Learning Lab, visit https://pvl.cs.princeton.edu/

media:group.media:title: Save the Cactus!
media:group.media:description:
This group of incoming first-year engineering students spent a good part of their summer trying to save a cactus. It wasn’t a real cactus, but the physics problem was real: How could they use a drone to tip or tilt this basket over before it falls upon the cactus? They created hooks for a drone that would, if successful, tip the basket over and then detach under the weight of the basket, so the rescue mission doesn’t end in a crash.
It was part of an engineering course offered by the Freshman Scholars Institute and taught by Claire Gmachl, the Eugene Higgins Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, with help from Leigh Cole of the Engineering Quad’s new Tiger Works makerspace.
Gmachl said the challenge taught students two skills essential to engineers: problem solving and building things. While the groups eventually found success, it happened after a lot of trial and error, learning, design and redesign, she said. The exercise, she said, taught the students about "staying goal oriented and resilient.”

media:group.media:title: Ryan's tricked-out trumpet
media:group.media:description:
Ryan Gonzales ’26 introduces us to the tricked-out trumpet that serves as his senior thesis project. An electronic wind instrument is played like an ordinary instrument, but instead of traditional acoustics, when a musician blows into it, the instrument produces sound through electronic synthesis. They offer a much wider variety of sounds, providing more creative freedom to the musician.
However, existing products more closely resemble woodwind instruments, and the way they are played is very different from the way that a brass instrument would be played. So Ryan, a mechanical and aerospace engineering major, worked on using this trumpet to collect data that could be used someday to develop a version more comfortable for brass players. His sensing device uses pressure transducers, strain gauges, a camera, and a microphone to take measurements, such as the applied force on the mouthpiece. It stores this data for the future development of a model that can make predictions of the pitch, dynamic, and articulation of a note being produced. Such a model could be used to develop electronic wind instruments that use brass mouthpieces, providing a more familiar experience to brass musicians, and taking into account the musician's embouchure when outputting audio.
Ryan's advisors were Jeffrey Snyder (music) and Joshua Shaevitz (physics). Over the past three years, Ryan has been a sound technician, engineer, and, most recently, sound designer for the Princeton Triangle Club. He has also worked as both a sound design mentor and audio engineer for the Lewis Center for the Arts. Now that he's graduated, Ryan hopes to work in the field of acoustics, exploring interests in audio systems and equipment design, and has future plans to obtain a master's degree in the field.

entry.title: Using brain cells to do computation

media:group.media:title: Using brain cells to do computation
media:group.media:description:
Princeton researchers have combined brain cells and advanced electronics into a 3D device that can be programmed to recognize patterns using computational techniques.
Past attempts at using brain cells to do computation have relied on 2D cultures grown in a petri dish or 3D clusters that are probed and monitored from outside. The Princeton device takes a different approach, working from the inside out.
In this video, Kumar Mritunjay, a postdoc in Electrical and Computer Engineering and first author of a new paper in Nature Electronics, talks about the work.

media:group.media:title: Origami and tensegrity
media:group.media:description:
Termite mounds are remarkable structures that regulate temperature, balance airflow and maintain structural stability in some of Earth’s harshest climates. And like other irregular, disordered systems, they can be difficult to replicate with modern engineering techniques.
Now, researchers at Princeton’s engineering school have developed a system for designers to mimic irregular natural structures like termite mounds or human bones — not only their microstructural patterns, but their mechanical properties as well.
“We created a theory that is applicable to two distinct physical systems,” said Glaucio Paulino, the Margareta Engman Augustine Professor of Engineering at Princeton. “Knowing one such system can help to understand the other one better.”
In an article published March 19 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the researchers explain how they developed the method by combining two disciplines: origami, which studies how surfaces fold along creases; and tensegrity, which explores structures held together by compression and tension. Origami is commonly used to create objects that fold into compact shapes and expand to deploy in tasks such as space exploration. Tensegrity describes structures like the human skeleton, which holds its shape through a balanced distribution of stress among hard bones and soft tissues.
By exploring the mathematics that govern origami and tensegrity, the researchers learned that the systems’ underlying math rules are essentially the same. Although not obvious to non-mathematicians, the formula governing origami’s precise folds can be translated into the rules that govern tensegrity’s force distribution.
“It turns out that the same equation describes both engineering structures, origami and tensegrity,” said Xiangxin Dang, a postdoctoral researcher at Princeton and the article’s first author. “These two different types of structures are connected by math.”
Regular shapes, such as a cube or a sphere, are easy to design because they can be described by a small number of variables, Dang said. But irregular shapes, such as a termite mound or a complex section of bone, can demand many such variables to describe such disordered systems. This can make some designs impractical because these variables form large systems of equations demanding extensive analysis.

entry.title: Alexander Liou's blended-wing body aircraft senior thesis project

media:group.media:title: Alexander Liou's blended-wing body aircraft senior thesis project
media:group.media:description: Alexander Liou ’26 showed us his advanced aircraft that serves as his senior thesis project, currently in its final stages of production in the Engineering Quadrangle’s machine shop. Most aircraft use a tube-and-wing design, but what Alex is creating is a blended-wing body aircraft that combines the wings and fuselage into a single aerodynamic shape. The design reduces drag, provides more lift, and requires less power. This drone is designed to take off vertically, using two 13-inch propellers mounted on the motors. Alex says that he originally designed this prototype as a potential way to deliver blood products to medics more efficiently than a conventional "multicopter"; the drone’s payload size allows for transport of four 250ml blood packages. He said it could someday also be used for rapid response search and rescue, or low-risk military reconnaissance. His major is mechanical and aerospace engineering, and his advisers are Luigi Martinelli and Clarence Rowley.

entry.title: Training workers to make the next generation of computer chips

media:group.media:title: Training workers to make the next generation of computer chips
media:group.media:description:
Thanks to a collaboration between Princeton and Mercer County Community College, we can train more workers in the techniques needed to make the next generation of computer chips.
Students at MCCC teamed up with Bert Harrop of the Princeton Materials Institute and developed a digital simulation of the chipmaking facility that Harrop leads at PMI’s Advanced Micro Assembly and Packaging Lab. This “digital twin” simulates the state-of-the-art equipment at PMI and is a cost-effective way for technicians to build their skills. “It’s affordable. You don’t need to go into an expensive machine until you really need to,” said Prof. Shianling Wu, the students’ advisor at MCCC.

entry.title: Technology-enhanced player piano Name That Tune!

media:group.media:title: Technology-enhanced player piano Name That Tune!
media:group.media:description: We recently checked back in with Samuel Gerhard, a graduate student in electrical and computer engineering who was working to install modern technology in a 19th-century player piano. Sam restored the antique instrument as part of his senior thesis before his graduation last spring, outfitting it with computerized capabilities to play any song on command. He now has the player piano outfitted with a combination of MIDI (musical instrument digital interface technology) software, digital circuits, and mechanical hardware to enable the instrument to play almost anything. Can you guess the songs the piano is playing? Put your guesses in the comments. This video shows what he’s been able to do. You can see our original video about Sam’s senior thesis at this link: https://lnkd.in/eCb-GM2e
